title: How Tipping Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss tipping: its possible origins (sixteenth-century European servant tips, "drinking money" etymology), how it took hold in the US via the Pullman Company underpaying porters, tipped minimum wage laws and the proposed HR 31 Wages Act, Cornell research on what increases tips (touching, squatting, candy, sunny weather talk), tipping guidelines for many service workers (hotels, bellhops, concierges, valets, mechanics, delivery people, manicurists, hairdressers, bartenders, sommeliers), people who don't need tipping, celebrity tipping reputations, and listener mail about Viking holmgang duels.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener poll on tipping annoyances
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about their waiting experience and joke about tipping; they discuss which services listeners find most annoying to tip for, such as bathroom attendants, takeout, salons and coffee house tip jars.

segments.title: Tipped minimum wage and coffee shop tipping debate
segments.summary: The hosts explain the federal tipped minimum wage, state variations such as Colorado, the Fair Eats group, and argue about whether employers make up the difference and whether tipping at coffee shops and fast food is appropriate.

segments.title: Origins of tipping
segments.summary: Theories of tipping's origin: sixteenth-century European visitors tipping servants, and the 'drinking money' etymology. The hosts dismiss the acronym 'to insure promptness' story and note the word tip in other languages means drinking money.

segments.title: Pullman porters and tipping in the United States
segments.summary: Tipping was not widespread in the US until the Pullman Company relied on customer tips to pay its porters, saving money on payroll. The hosts discuss the restaurant owner argument about wages and turnover.
topics: tipping history in the United States

segments.title: Psychology of tipping and Cornell research
segments.summary: Discussion of why people tip, citing guilt and fear, and Cornell research finding the US leads the world in neuroticism and extroversion, linking these traits to bigger tips.

segments.title: Server tactics that increase tips
segments.summary: Cornell studies on server behaviors: brief touching, squatting to eye level, giving candy, and describing sunny weather, with tip percentage changes cited. The hosts also discuss tipping on the original amount when coupons are used and tipping on wine.

segments.title: Tipping guide for restaurants, bars, and other service workers
segments.summary: Guidance on tipping the maître d', sommelier, bartenders, buffet and cafeteria staff, and the practice of pooled tips. The hosts also cover coffee shops and charity requests at grocery checkouts.

segments.title: Holiday tipping and everyday service tipping
segments.summary: Guidance on holiday tips for service providers such as garbage collectors, nannies, manicurists and hairdressers, plus hotel maids, bellhops and concierges, doormen, and delivery drivers.

segments.title: Tipping mechanics, valets, skycaps, airport and flight staff, and who not to tip
segments.summary: Tipping guidance for valets, skycaps, taxi drivers, mechanics, gas station attendants, and international tipping. Also covers people who do not need tips, such as restaurant owners, flight attendants and fast food employees, and the federal tipped wage bill HR 31.

segments.title: Celebrity tipping reputations
segments.summary: The hosts read lists of celebrity good and bad tippers, noting the stories are unverified; examples include Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, David Byrne and Michael Moore.

segments.title: Listener mail: Viking holmgang duels
segments.summary: A listener from Minnesota describes the Viking holmgang, a duel on an ox hide with shields and axes, and the hosts plug the How Vikings Were episode and the show's social channels.
